Senses.Explanation: A code is a binding body of rules, its regulated conduct, and the institutional offices that transmit and interpret it. Chan records cite code provisions in public interviews, assign named precept specialists, adapt communal standards to circumstances, and preserve arguments over whether code can be dismissed. The Platform Record’s ordination account distinguishes the Vinaya-master roles: Zhiguang bestows the precepts, Huijing conducts the formal act, Tongying instructs, and Jiduoluo recites the precepts. Yaoshan Weiyan declines an expected address by saying, ‘scriptures have scripture masters; rules have Vinaya masters’ (經有經師，律有律師), while another exchange begins, ‘the code says that hearing ornaments through a wall is called breaking the precepts’ (律中道。隔壁聞釵釧聲即名破戒) and then asks whether a crowded visual scene is or is not precept-breaking. The Baizhang account records a specifically Chan institutional bend: asked why he did not simply follow an existing greater-vehicle precept code, he says his tradition is neither confined to nor different from the greater and lesser vehicles, calls for standards fitted to circumstances, and establishes a separate Chan residence. The Record of the Source-Mirror says, ‘all one’s doings enter regulated conduct’ (所有施為，皆入律行). Yongjue also records and rebukes the dismissal, ‘holding and breaking are originally absent—what use are precepts and code?’ (本無持犯，何用戒律？). The headword therefore remains concrete code-language while Chan records assign it offices, cite it in interview, fit communal standards to circumstances, extend it to conduct, and preserve arguments over its cancellation.
Senses.Note: Flyswatter-test deviation: code-language is not excluded as generic non-Chan religious vocabulary; the Baizhang record deploys it in the founding description of a separate Chan residence. Exact count: 3,110 hits in 360 files.

Occurrences.Kwic: 西京智光律師為授戒師，蘇州慧靜律師為羯磨，荊州通應律師為教授，中天耆多羅律師為說戒，西國蜜多三藏為證戒。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (六祖大師法寶壇經), Outer Record of the Sixth Patriarch's Origins (六祖大師緣起外紀). The section is explicitly compiled by the disciple Fahai and others (門人法海等集); Fahai is the named lead compiler narrating the five ordination offices, while Huineng is the recipient and biographical subject, not the narrator.

Occurrences.Kwic: 或曰。瑜伽論瓔珞經。是大乘戒律。胡不依隨哉。師曰。吾所宗非局大小乘。非異大小乘。當博約折中設於制範務其宜也。於是創意別立禪居。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Exact actor: Baizhang Huaihai. Source text (景德傳燈錄). Asked why he does not follow the greater-vehicle precept code, Baizhang says rules are fitted to circumstances and a separate Chan residence is established.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Exact actor: Yongming Yanshou. Source text (宗鏡錄). The Record of the Source-Mirror says all doings enter regulated conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：經有經師，律有律師，爭怪得老僧？丹霞天然禪師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings (御選語錄), Yaoshan Weiyan section. Yaoshan Weiyan is the exact speaker who distinguishes scripture and Vinaya specialists after declining to deliver the expected address.

Occurrences.Kwic: 律中道。隔壁聞釵釧聲即名破戒。見覩金銀合雜朱紫駢闐。是破戒不是破戒。師曰。好箇入路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp (景德傳燈錄): inside Daoqian's biography, Fayan Wenyi is the exact questioner denoted by Jinghui who cites the Vinaya rule about hearing ornaments through a wall and asks whether seeing the gathered colors and precious metals is breaking the precepts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本無持犯，何用戒律？因果罪福，一切滅裂。至於貪名奪利，有如狂狗；恃氣起爭，不啻猛虎。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Exact actor: Yongjue Yuanxian. Source text (永覺元賢禪師廣錄). Yongjue quotes and rebukes the claim that precepts and code are useless because holding and breaking are originally absent.

Senses.Explanation: In the compound (音律), (律) denotes regulated sound, meter, or tonal pattern rather than a monastic code. A Chan verse says that an old tune is not reducible to musical regulation before turning to the South Mountain turtle-nosed snake; two major lamp compilations preserve that deployment. Modern scholarly body prose in the allowlisted corpus likewise judges a song's musical regulation sound while rejecting its wording. The shared object is ordering of sound, not ordained conduct.
Senses.Note: This is a different referent from Vinaya or communal code. C077 and C078 preserve related recensions of one Chan verse; B25n0143 supplies an independent body-prose witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打皷弄琵琶相逢一會家雲門能合調長慶解隨邪古曲非音律南山鼈鼻蛇何人知妙訣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄): Zhenjing Kewen is the author of the verse on the Xuefeng turtle-nosed-snake case that says the old tune is not a musical measure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 打鼓弄琵琶相逢一會家雲門能合調長慶觧隨邪古曲非音律南山鼈鼻蛇何人知妙訣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Connected Anthology of Verses on Old Chan Cases (禪宗頌古聯珠通集): the inline contributor note 'Zhenjing's text' (真淨文) assigns this verse to Zhenjing Kewen; he likens the exchange to drum and lute in concert, then says the old tune is not musical measure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然「音律不差」，而「下語用字，全不可讀」，也沒有文學價值
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Third Dunhuang Manuscript of Shenhui's Recorded Sayings: Miscellaneous Questions and Answers of the Nanyang Preceptor, Collected by Liu Cheng (神會和尚語錄的第三個敦煌寫本：南陽和尚問答雜徵義（劉澄集）), in Hu Shi's modern scholarly postscript on the five-watch songs. Hu Shi is the exact prose author who says that the songs' musical regulation is not deficient but their wording and character choice are unreadable and lack literary value. The inline note credits the following wording judgment to Shen Yifu's Yuefu Zhimi; Shenhui is the manuscript subject, not the speaker of this modern sentence.
